title: Rash and Lethargy
hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a 6-year-old child who presents with fever, sore throat, malaise, and generalized rash. Exam reveals posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, palatal petechiae, and splenomegaly. The combination of pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, fever, and the characteristic maculopapular rash is classic for infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus. The differential includes other viral infections (CMV, acute HIV), streptococcal pharyngitis, and toxoplasmosis. Key management considerations: avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin (causes characteristic EBV rash), avoid aspirin (Reye syndrome risk in febrile children), and in older patients, restrict contact sports to prevent splenic rupture.

stacks.finding: Heterophil antibody (Monospot) or EBV-specific serology confirms the diagnosis.

stacks.finding: BMPs are excellent screening tools. LFTs may show elevated transaminases in EBV hepatitis.

stacks.label: Acetaminophen / Ibuprofen
stacks.finding: Tylenol or ibuprofen for fever reduction. Symptomatic management.

stacks.label: Aspirin, therapy
stacks.finding: Administering aspirin to a febrile child is associated with Reye's syndrome. Contraindicated.

stacks.label: Amoxicillin / Ampicillin
stacks.finding: In EBV, amoxicillin and ampicillin cause a characteristic morbilliform rash. Viral infection — antibiotics ineffective. Especially avoid these two.

stacks.label: Advise patient, no aspirin
stacks.finding: Important to tell caregiver not to give aspirin to the febrile child.

physical_exam.heent: Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Palatal petechiae. Pharyngeal erythema with tonsillar exudates.

decoys.reason_wrong: Causes characteristic morbilliform rash in EBV infection. Viral — antibiotics ineffective.

decoys.label: Aspirin
decoys.reason_wrong: Associated with Reye's syndrome in febrile children. Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen instead.

decoys.reason_wrong: Splenomegaly diagnosis is clinical. CT not indicated unless splenic rupture suspected.

teach_me_steps.order: Recognize classic triad: fever + pharyngitis + lymphadenopathy
teach_me_steps.reasoning: EBV mononucleosis presents with sore throat (often with palatal petechiae), fever, malaise, posterior cervical adenopathy, and splenomegaly.
Heterophil antibody test (Monospot) is screening; EBV-specific IgM/IgG confirms in young children who may be Monospot-negative.
Ampicillin and amoxicillin cause a characteristic drug rash in EBV. Viral infection does not require antibiotics.
Aspirin in febrile children is associated with Reye's syndrome. Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen.
Uncomplicated mononucleosis can be managed as outpatient. Hospitalization only if airway compromise or splenic rupture.

case_summary: Classic pediatric mononucleosis. Fever + pharyngitis + lymphadenopathy + splenomegaly. Monospot/EBV serology confirms. Symptomatic treatment: acetaminophen, rest. Avoid aspirin (Reye's) and amoxicillin/ampicillin (drug rash). Office management.
